la:noun:aditus.html:
ădĭtus, ūs, m.
1. adeo
,
a going to, approach, access.
Lit.: quorum abitu aut aditu,: urbes permultas uno aditu atque adventu esse captas,: quo neque sit ventis aditus,; so —With ad: aditus ad eum difficilior,; so ; ; .—With in (cf. 1. adeo): aditus in id sacrarium non est viris,; so Auct. Or. pro Dom. 42, 110 al.: aditus ad me minime provinciales, which are not made in the manner customary (with the prœtor), .—
Transf.
The possibility, leave, permission, or right of approaching, or of admittance, access (cf. accessus): faciles aditus ad eum privatorum,; so ; ; ; ; : homo rari aditūs,a man rarely accessible,.—Trop.: si qui mihi erit aditus de tuis fortunis agendi,; so ; .—
Coner., the place through which one approaches a thing, an entrance, avenue, etc. (opp. abitus; cf. also accessus): primo aditu vestibuloque prohibere,; : aditus insulae muniti,; so ; ; ; ; ; ; .—Hence trop. (in Cic. very freq.): quartus aditus ad initia rerum, Müll.: aditus ad causam,: vestibula honesta aditusque ad causam illustres facere,; so ; ; ; ; ; ;

la:verb:adipiscor.gloss: to arrive at, reach; overtake, catch up with
senses: to arrive at, reach; overtake, catch up with
to get, obtain, acquire, get possession of, achieve, attain
la:verb:adipiscor.html:
ăd-ĭpiscor, eptus, 3, v. dep.
apiscor
,
to arrive at, to reach.
Lit.: occepi sequi; vix adipiscendi potestas fuit,.—Hence also with acc., to reach, to overtake: fugientes Gallos Macedones adepti ceciderunt,; cf. Drak. ad .—Far oftener,
Fig., to attain to by effort, to get, obtain, acquire, to get possession of (by overcoming natural obstacles; diff. from impetrare, to reach or obtain by victory over another's will; and nancisci, by accident, Doed. Syn. III. pp. 145, 146; IV. p. 369): nuptias effugere ego istas malo quam tu adipiscier,: senectutem ut adipiscantur, omnes optant; eandem accusant adepti,: summos honores a populo Romano,: amplissimos dignitatis gradus,: gloriam,; : quanta instrumenta (homo) habeat ad obtinendam adipiscendamque sapientiam,; so ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; .— With ex: adeptum esse omnia e natura et animo et corpore et vitā,; cf. ; .—With ut. adepti sunt, ut dies festos agitare possent, .—Absol.: non potestis adipisci,.!*?
iis adipiscendi magistratus, they should strive for public honors (the consequens for the antecedens), .—
Nero in adipiscenda morte (Epaphroditi) manu adjutus existimabatur, i. e. consciscenda, in committing suicide, Oud.; cf. ; ; and: invenire mortem,. —
Pass.: non aetate, verum ingenio, adipiscitur sapientia,: haec

adipiscuntur, C. Fannius ap. P.: amitti magis quam adipisci, Fab. Maximus, ib.; so esp. adeptus,; ; ; ; ; cf. ; ; Rudd. I. p. 288; Kritz ad .—

With gen.: arma, quīs Galba rerum adeptus est,; (here Halm reads apisceretur); Rudd. II. p. 120; Zumpt, § 466.

la:verb:adimo.html:
ăd-ĭmo, ēmi, emptum, 3, v. a.
emo
(adempsit = ademerit, ),
to take to one's self from a person or thing, to take away, take any thing from, to deprive of (syn.: demere, eximere, auterre, eripere).
Of things: si ego memorem quae me erga fecisti bene, nox diem adimat,would take away, consume,: multa ferunt anni venientes commoda secum; multa recedentes adimunt, take them away with themselves, as a fine antithesis to secum ferunt, : ut istas compedes tibi adimam, huic dem,: metum,; so ; ; : Juppiter, ingentes qui das adimisque dolores,: animam,: postquam adempta spes est,: alicui vitam,: pecuniam,: somnum,: libertatem,: exercitum,: aditum litoris,: omnia sociis,: arma militibus,: vires ad vincendum,: imperium,: pernicitatem,.—And absol.: Qui propter invidiam adimunt diviti,.—Poet. with inf. as object: adimam cantare severis, (cf. Gr. ἀφαιρήσομαι ἀείδειν, I will prohibit them to sing; so ; ).—
Poet. of persons, to snatch away, to carry off: hanc, nisi mors, mihi adimet nemo,: virgo, quae puellas audis adimisque leto,.—(For the distinction between demere, adimere, eximere, v. Lamb. ad ; cf. ; Bentl. ; and cf. Doed. Syn. IV. pp. 123-126.)

la:verb:adigo.html:
ăd-ĭgo, ēgi, actum, 3, v. a.
ago
(adaxint = adegerint, ; ; cf. adaxi for adegi),
to drive, bring, or take a person or thing to a place (syn.: appello, adduco, affero).—Constr. usu. with ad, but also with acc., dat., in or local adv.
Lit., of cattle (cf. ago, I.: abigo, abigeus, etc.): quis has huc ovīs adegit?: lactantes vitulos ad matres,: pecore e longinquioribus vicis adacto,: equos per publicum,. —Of persons: mox noctu te adiget horsum insomnia,: aliquem fulmine ad umbras,: quis deus Italiam vos adegit?.—Hence: adigere aliquem arbitrum (ad arbitrum), to compel one to come before an arbiter (like adigere (ad) jus jurandum; v.infra): finibus regundis adigere arbitrum non possis,; so ; .—Of things: classem e Ponto Byzantium adigi jusserat,: ceteras navium per fossas,, and absol.: dum adiguntur naves, i. e. in mare impelluntur,: tigna fistucis,to drive in by rammers,.—Esp. often of weapons, to drive home, plunge, thrust, to send to a place: ut felum adigi non posset,; cf. ; so ; : hastae ardentes adactae,: ferrum jugulo,: cf. : per obscena ferrum,: ferrum in viscera,.— And from the weapons transf. to the wound, to inflict (in the poets and Tac.): alte vulnus adactum,: ubi vulnus Varo adactum,: vulnus per galeam adegit,.
Fig.
To drive, urge, or bring one to a situation, to a state of mind, or to an act (esp. against his will): tu, homo, adigis me ad insaniam,: adigit ita Postumia,: acri cupidine adigi,: ad mortem,.—Poet. with the subj. without ut: quae vis vim mihi afferam ipsa adigit,.—With the inf.: vertere morsus exiguam in Cererem penuria adegit edendi, ; cf. 6, 696; so ; ; .— So also: tres liburnicas adactis per vim gubernatoribus ascendere,; so ; ; .—
Adigere aliquem ad jus jurandum, jus jurandum, or jure jurando, or sacramento (abl.), t. t., to put one on oath, to cause one to take oath, to swear one (from the time of Livy oftener with abl.; so Tac.. Just., Flor.; cf. on this point Cortius ad ; Held ad ; Herz. ad ; Rudd. II. p. 328, no. 16): omnibus jus jurandum adactis,: cum ad jus jurandum populares sceleris sui adigeret,: provinciam omnem in sua et Pompeii verba jus jurandum adigebat,: censores ita jus jurandum adigebant,; so ; : populum jure jurando adegit,: omnibus junioribus jure jurando adactis,; so 6, 38; 7, 9, 11 al.; ; ; ; ; .—Hence ellipt.: in verba adigere, for in verba jus jurandum adigere in Tac. and Suet. (cf. the passage cited above, ): neque se neque quemquam Batavum in verba Galliarum adegit,: provincia Narbon. in verba Vitellii adacta,; so 4, 59; .— And finally quite absol.: adigere (sc. jure jurando, sacramento), to bind by an oath: magno cum assensu auditus ... universos adigit,.—
Poet. = subigere, to subject: bisque jugo Rhenum, bis adactum legibus Istrum,: in faciem prorae pinus adacta novae,brought into the form of a ship,.!*? In : mare quod adigit ad ostium Rhodani, we have a false reading, for which Nipperdey restored adjacet.

la:verb:adimpleo.html:
ăd-implĕo, ēvi, ētum, 2, v. a.,
to fill up, to fill full (in the class. per., e. g. in , and , dub.).
Lit.: Gangem decem fluminibus adimpleri, Aethic. Cosmogr. p. 709 ed. Gron.: quasi mare adimpleti sunt,.—
Trop.: adimpleti tibiarum cantu vocant deam suam, Jul. Firm. de Err. p. 10 (cf. adimpletor): adimplebis me laetitiā,.—
Metaph., to fulfil (as a promise, prediction, duty), to perform, = absolvere, satisfacere, praestare: aliquid,: quod dictum est,: ut adimpleatur scriptura,: legem Christi,: Gratia vobis et pax adimpleatur,be made full, perfect, Pet. 1, 2.

la:verb:adiuvo#4.html:
ad-jŭvo, jūvi, jūtum, 1, v. a. (very rare juvavi, juvatum;
hence, adjuvaturus,: adjŭro or adjuero = adjuvero, Enn. ap. : adjuerit = adjuverit,), to give aid to, to help, assist, support: aliquem. (Adjuvare applies to every kind of help or support; while auxiliari is only used of one who, from his weakness, needs assistance, and subvenire of one who is in difficulty or embarrassment; cf. Manut. ad .)
In gen.: O Tite, si quid te adjuero curamve levāsso quae nunc te coquit, etc., Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 339 Vahl.): di me etsi perdunt, tamen esse adjutam expetunt, Pac. ap. (R): miseras, inopes, aerumnosas aliquo auxilio,: operā me adjuves,: me adjuves in hac re,: id spero adjuturos deos (i. e. in ea re),: ad verum probandum auctoritas adjuvat,: si nihil ad percipiendam colendamque virtutem litteris adjuvarentur,: maerorem orationis lacrimis suis, id. de Or.

2, 47: Q. Hortensii operā rem publicam adjutam (esse),: si nos mediocris fortuna rei publicae adjuverit, Planc. ap. : aliquem in filiarum collocatione,: auxiliis et copiis, i. e. militibus auxiliariis,; cf. : sua sponte eos adjutum profectus,; ; : Antiochum Aetolosque adjuturos pronuntiat,: fortĭs fortuna adjuvat,, and : aliquem ad bellum,; cf. Drak.: adjutus casu,: suffragio,: manu alicujus,: adjuvare preces,: pennis adjutus amoris,; so ; ; cf. .—

Esp.
To help, cherish (esp. a state of mind), to sustain: jam tu quoque hujus adjuvas insaniam,: ferendus error immo vero etiam adjuvandus,: clamore Romani adjuvant militem suum,animate, encourage,; so : ignem,: formam cură,.—
Absol. (very rare), to profit, avail, be of use, be profitable (syn.: utile est, operae pretium est, convenit).
Impers.: in re mala animo si bono utare, adjuvat,.—
With subject: solitudo aliquid adjuvat,: alteri non multum adjuvabant,: adjuvat hoc quoque,.!*? Rare constructions.
With a whole subjective clause with quod as subject: multum eorum opinionem adjuvat, quod (the circumstance that) sine jumentis ... ad iter profectos videbant, . —
With two acc.: irrides in re tanta? neque me quidquam consilio adjuvas?; cf. Rudd. II. p. 179, n. 75.—
With ut or ne: ut amplissimum nomen consequeremur, unus praeter ceteros adjuvisti,: adjuvato, nequis liminis obseret tabellam,.—
With inf.: adjuvat enim (pater, the male) incubare, helps to hatch, .—
With the dat. of the person and the acc. of the thing: operam mutuam dent et messem hanc nobis adjuvent,; cf. adjuto.—Hence, adjŭvans, antis, P. a., subst. with gen.: non haec adjuvantia causarum, sed has ipsas esse omnium causas,.

la:verb:adinvenio.html:
ăd-invĕnĭo, vēni, ventum, 4, v. a.
ad, intens.
,
to find out, to devise, ; ; cf. also : lapicaedinae adinventae sunt, Labi Ins.: si quis ainventus (for adinventus) fuerit hoc fecisse, Mur. Ins. 794.

senses: to turn the eyes pryingly to
la:verb:adiicio#4.html:
ad-jĭcĭo (better adicio), jēci, jectum, 3, v. a.
jacio
,
to throw or cast a thing to, to put or place at or near.—Constr.: aliquid alicui rei.
In gen.: rogum bustumve novum vetat propius sexaginta pedes adici aedes alienas,to place nearer than,: hordei numero ad summam tritici adjecto,: adjectoque cavae supplentur sanguine venae,; so ; .— More freq. trop.: quo ne imprudentiam quidem oculorum adici fas fuit, to turn the eyes pryingly to, to direct the sight to, etc., : Parthus adjecit Armeniae manum,: album calculum errori,to approve,. —With in: virus in anguīs,: telum ex locis superioribus in litus,to throw, to hurl,.—
Transf. to mental objects, to turn or direct the mind, eye, etc., to, to fasten them upon something.—With dat. or ad: qui amabilitati animum adiceret,: animum militi,: ad virginem animum adjecit,: cum ad omnia vestra pauci homines cupiditatis oculos adjecissent,: plane videbant adjectum esse oculum hereditati, (diff. from adicere oculos, cited above): adjecit animum ad consilium,: novo etiam consilio animum adjecit,.—
Esp.
To add or apply to a thing by way of increase, to increase, = προστιθέναι (cf. addo).—Lit. and trop.; constr. with ad or dat.: ad bellicam laudem ingenii gloriam,: decus alicui,: aliquantum ea res duci famae et auctoritatis adjecit,: so ; ; ; ; ; ; : morem ritusque sacrorum adiciam,: adjecere bonae paulo plus artis Athenac,; so ; id. P. l, 8, 56; and 33; also to add a new thought to what has preceded (cf.: addo, accedo, advenio; hence, like addo, in the sing., though several persons are addressed): huc natas adice septem,.—
Of a speaker, to add to what has already been said. —Constr. with acc. and inf. (only in Vell. and in the histt. after the Aug. per.): adiciens numquam defuturos raprores Italicae libertatis lupos,; so, adjecerat Tiberius non id tempus censurae nec defuturum corrigendi auctorem,: adjecit in domo ejus venenum esse,.—Rarely followed by orat. directa: cum dixisset ... adjecissetque: Si quid huic acciderit, etc.,.—With ut and subj., .—
In anctions, t. t., to add to a bid, to out-bid: liciti sunt usque adeo, quoad se efficere posse arbitrabantur; super adjecit Aeschrio,bid on, B. and K.; but cf. Zumpt ad h. l.; .—
In gen., in the Vulg. by Hebraism (cf. ), to add to do, to do further: adjecit Dominus loqui, the Lord furthermore spake, Isa. 7, 10: non adiciet, ut resurgat, ib. 24, 20: adiciens dixit parabolam,.

In gen.: rogum bustumve novum vetat propius sexaginta pedes adici aedes alienas,to place nearer than,: hordei numero ad summam tritici adjecto,: adjectoque cavae supplentur sanguine venae,; so ; .— More freq. trop.: quo ne imprudentiam quidem oculorum adici fas fuit, to turn the eyes pryingly to, to direct the sight to, etc., : Parthus adjecit Armeniae manum,: album calculum errori,to approve,. —With in: virus in anguīs,: telum ex locis superioribus in litus,to throw, to hurl,.—
Transf. to mental objects, to turn or direct the mind, eye, etc., to, to fasten them upon something.—With dat. or ad: qui amabilitati animum adiceret,: animum militi,: ad virginem animum adjecit,: cum ad omnia vestra pauci homines cupiditatis oculos adjecissent,: plane videbant adjectum esse oculum hereditati, (diff. from adicere oculos, cited above): adjecit animum ad consilium,: novo etiam consilio animum adjecit,.—
Esp.
To add or apply to a thing by way of increase, to increase, = προστιθέναι (cf. addo).—Lit. and trop.; constr. with ad or dat.: ad bellicam laudem ingenii gloriam,: decus alicui,: aliquantum ea res duci famae et auctoritatis adjecit,: so ; ; ; ; ; ; : morem ritusque sacrorum adiciam,: adjecere bonae paulo plus artis Athenac,; so ; id. P. l, 8, 56; and 33; also to add a new thought to what has preceded (cf.: addo, accedo, advenio; hence, like addo, in the sing., though several persons are addressed): huc natas adice septem,.—
Of a speaker, to add to what has already been said. —Constr. with acc. and inf. (only in Vell. and in the histt. after the Aug. per.): adiciens numquam defuturos raprores Italicae libertatis lupos,; so, adjecerat Tiberius non id tempus censurae nec defuturum corrigendi auctorem,: adjecit in domo ejus venenum esse,.—Rarely followed by orat. directa: cum dixisset ... adjecissetque: Si quid huic acciderit, etc.,.—With ut and subj., .—
In anctions, t. t., to add to a bid, to out-bid: liciti sunt usque adeo, quoad se efficere posse arbitrabantur; super adjecit Aeschrio,bid on, B. and K.; but cf. Zumpt ad h. l.; .—
In gen., in the Vulg. by Hebraism (cf. ), to add to do, to do further: adjecit Dominus loqui, the Lord furthermore spake, Isa. 7, 10: non adiciet, ut resurgat, ib. 24, 20: adiciens dixit parabolam,.

la:adj:adipatus.html:
ădĭpātus, a, um, adj.
adeps
,
filled or supplied with fat, fatty, greasy.
Lit.: puls, Lucil. ap. and 74 P.; hence, absol.: ădĭpātum (sc. edulium), i, pastry prepared with fat (cf. Charis. l. c.): livida materno fervent adipata veneno,.—
Trop. of discourse, coarse, gross: opimum quoddam et tamquam adipatae orationis genus,; also ap. (al. adipale).
